title: What Can You Do? Skills and Abilities
description: Learn to talk about your skills, abilities, and what you are still learning
objectives: Say what you can and cannot do
Talk about skills you are learning
Connect personal skills to work situations

phrases: I know how to [fix cars/speak Arabic]
I can't ... yet, but I'm learning
target_language.grammar_pattern:
Can / Can't
  I can drive. → I am able to drive.
  I can't speak French. → I am not able to speak French.
  Can you cook? → Are you able to cook?

Know how to
  I know how to use a computer.
  I don't know how to swim yet.

Good at + verb-ing
  I'm good at cooking.
  She's good at organizing things.

grammar_patterns.label: Ability with CAN
examples: I can lift heavy boxes.
I can speak Somali and English.
I can't drive yet, but I'm learning.
Can you use a computer?

grammar_patterns.label: Know how to
examples: I know how to cook Somali food.
She knows how to fix motorcycles.
I don't know how to use this machine yet.
Do you know how to drive a forklift?

grammar_patterns.label: Good at + verb-ing
examples: I'm good at organizing things.
He's good at working with customers.
Are you good at lifting heavy things?
I'm not very good at speaking on the phone yet.

story.context: Ahmed meets his neighbor Carlos, who works at a warehouse. Carlos is helping Ahmed think about his skills before he starts looking for a job.

dialogue.speaker: Carlos
dialogue.text: Ahmed! You've been here a few months now. Are you thinking about finding a job?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: Yes, I want to find work soon. But I don't know what jobs I can do.

dialogue.speaker: Carlos
dialogue.text: Let's think about your skills. Can you drive?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: Yes, I can drive. I drove a truck in Somalia for five years.

dialogue.speaker: Carlos
dialogue.text: Good! That's a real skill. Can you use a computer?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: A little. I know how to use email. I'm still learning other programs.

dialogue.speaker: Carlos
dialogue.text: That's fine. What are you good at? What do people always ask you to help with?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: I'm good at organizing and lifting heavy things. I'm also good at working hard for a long time.

dialogue.speaker: Carlos
dialogue.text: Ahmed, you have more skills than you think. Can you work with other people on a team?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: Yes, I can. In Somalia, I always worked with a team.

dialogue.speaker: Carlos
dialogue.text: Then you are ready. You can drive, you can lift, you work in a team. You have skills!

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: I feel better now. Thank you, Carlos. I'm going to look for a job this week.

drills.title: Can and Can't
drills.instruction: Say what someone can or cannot do. Use: I can / I can't + [verb]
examples: I can speak two languages.
I can't drive a forklift yet.
She can cook very well.
He can't work on weekends.
Can you start on Monday?

drills.title: Know How To
drills.instruction: Say what you know how to do. Use: I know how to / I don't know how to + [verb]

prompts.sentence: I ___ how to cook Somali food. (yes)
She ___ how to use a cash register. (yes)
I ___ how to use that machine yet. (no)
___ you know how to drive a forklift?

examples: I know how to fix small machines.
I know how to speak three languages.
I don't know how to use that software yet.
She knows how to work the cash register.
Do you know how to drive a van?
drills.your_turn: Do you know how to drive a van?

drills.title: Good At
drills.instruction: Talk about what you are good at. Use: I'm good at / I'm not good at + [verb-ing]

prompts.sentence: I'm not very good at ___ on the phone. (speak)

examples: I'm good at organizing boxes.
I'm good at working in a team.
He's good at fixing things.
I'm not good at sitting all day.
Are you good at following instructions?
drills.your_turn: Are you good at following instructions?

listening.question: What can Maria do at her job?
listening.transcript: What can you do at your job, Maria? I can use a computer, and I am good at speaking with customers.
options: She can drive and use a forklift
She can only answer the phone
She can use a computer and speak to customers
listening.explanation: Maria says she can use a computer and she is good at speaking with customers. She does not drive or use a forklift.

listening.question: What skill is the speaker still learning?
listening.transcript: I can drive and I can cook, but I'm still learning how to use a computer.
listening.explanation: The speaker says 'I can drive and I can cook, but I'm still learning how to use a computer.' Computer skills are what they are still developing.

listening.question: Which skill does the employer ask about first?
listening.transcript: For this job, the most important thing is this: Can you lift 50 pounds?
listening.explanation: The job posting says the most important requirement is being able to lift 50 pounds. This is the first skill the employer asks about.

speaking.title: Your Skills List
speaking.instruction: Record yourself talking about 3 things you can do and 1 thing you are still learning. Use: I can..., I know how to..., I'm good at..., and I'm still learning...
speaking.example: I can drive a car. I know how to cook well. I'm good at lifting heavy things and working in a team. I'm still learning how to use a computer, but I practice every day.

speaking.title: Ask About Skills
speaking.instruction: Record yourself asking a friend about their abilities. Ask 3 questions using: Can you...?, Are you good at...?, and Do you know how to...?
speaking.example: Can you drive? Are you good at working with other people? Do you know how to use a cash register? These are useful skills for many jobs.

writing.title: My Skills
writing.instruction: Write 5 sentences about your skills and abilities. Include at least one thing you can do, one thing you know how to do, one thing you are good at, and one thing you are still learning.
writing.example: I can drive a truck. I know how to cook many different foods. I am good at organizing and keeping things clean. I can work in a team with no problems. I am still learning how to use a computer, but I practice every day.

writing.title: Skills for a Job
writing.instruction: Think about a job you want. Write 4 sentences explaining why your skills are good for that job. Use: I can, I know how to, I'm good at.
writing.example: I want to work in a warehouse. I can lift heavy boxes and I can drive a truck. I know how to organize and count things carefully. I am good at following instructions and working fast. I think I am ready for this job.

sections.title: CAN for ability
examples: I can drive. ✓
I can to drive. ✗ (never add 'to' after can)
She cans drive. ✗ (can never changes — no -s)
She can drive. ✓
Can you lift 50 pounds? ✓
Do you can lift 50 pounds? ✗
sections.question: What comes after CAN? Does CAN change for he/she?
sections.explanation: CAN is always followed by a base verb (no 'to'). CAN never adds -s, even for he/she/it. To ask a question, put CAN before the person: 'Can you...?' — never use 'do' with CAN.

sections.title: GOOD AT + verb-ing
examples: I'm good at organize. ✗
I'm good at organizing. ✓
She's good at lift. ✗
She's good at lifting. ✓
Are you good at speaking English? ✓
sections.question: What form does the verb take after 'good at'?
sections.explanation: After 'good at', the verb always ends in -ing (the gerund form). This is the same as after 'like', 'enjoy', and 'love'. Think: I like cooking → I'm good at cooking.

sections.title: CAN vs KNOW HOW TO
examples: I can swim. (natural, short)
I know how to swim. (more specific — I learned this skill)
I can cook. (general ability)
I know how to cook Somali food. (specific skill)
Do you know how to use this machine?
sections.question: What is the difference between 'can' and 'know how to'?
sections.explanation: 'Can' is general and natural for most situations. 'Know how to' emphasizes that you learned a specific skill. Both mean the same thing but 'know how to' sounds more deliberate, like a trained skill. In a job interview, 'I know how to operate a forklift' sounds more professional than 'I can operate a forklift.'

quiz.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: I can to drive a truck.
quiz.explanation: CAN is followed by the base verb only. No 'to', no -s, no -ing.

quiz.question: How do you ask about someone's skill using CAN?
quiz.explanation: To make a question with CAN, put CAN before the subject: 'Can you...?' Do NOT use 'do' with can.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: After 'good at', use verb-ing. Good at + organizing, lifting, cooking, speaking.

quiz.question: Ahmed says 'I'm still learning how to use a computer.' What does this mean?
options: He can use a computer very well.
He is not perfect yet, but he is improving.
He does not want to use computers.
quiz.explanation: 'I'm still learning' means the process is not finished — you are getting better but not expert yet. It is a positive, honest thing to say.

quiz.question: Which phrase is the most professional for a job interview?
options: I know how to operate a forklift.
I can to lift heavy things.
quiz.explanation: 'I know how to operate a forklift' is specific, professional, and grammatically correct. It shows you learned a specific skill.

quiz.question: What is the correct negative form?
quiz.explanation: The negative of CAN is CAN'T or CANNOT. Never use 'don't' with can.

quiz.question: Carlos asks Ahmed: '___ you work in a team?' What word goes in the blank?
quiz.explanation: We use CAN to ask about ability: 'Can you work in a team?' This asks whether Ahmed has the ability to work with others.

quiz.question: In the dialogue, what does Carlos help Ahmed realize?
options: Ahmed has no skills for work.
Ahmed needs to learn English first.
Ahmed has more skills than he thought.
Ahmed should not look for a job yet.
quiz.explanation: Carlos says 'You have more skills than you think.' He helps Ahmed see that driving, lifting, and teamwork are all valuable job skills.

quiz.question: Write 3 sentences about your own skills using: I can..., I know how to..., I'm good at...
quiz.explanation: Practice using all three ability structures: can + base verb, know how to + base verb, good at + verb-ing.

quiz.question: Think about a job you want. What one skill do you have that makes you good for that job? Explain in 2 sentences.
quiz.explanation: Connect your personal ability to a real job need. This is exactly what you will say in a job interview.

somali.description: Baro sida xirfadahaaga, kartidaada, iyo waxa aad weli baranayso looga hadlo
objectives: Sheeg waxa aad samayn karto iyo waxa aadan samayn karin

sections.explanation: CAN waxaa mar walba raaca fal aasaasi ah ('to' la'aan). CAN weligiis ma qaato -s, xitaa he/she/it. Su'aal, CAN geli qofka ka hor: 'Can you...?' — weligaa 'do' ha la isticmaalin CAN.
'good at' ka dib, falku mar walba wuxuu ku dhammaadaa -ing (qaabka gerund). Tani waa la mid tan ka dambaysa 'like', 'enjoy', iyo 'love'. Ka fikir: I like cooking → I'm good at cooking.

'Can' waa guud, waana dabiici xaalado badan. 'Know how to' waxay xoogga saaraysaa inaad baratay xirfad gaar ah. Labaduba isku macne bay leeyihiin, laakiin 'know how to' waxay u dhawaaqdaa xirfad la tababaray. Wareysiga shaqada, 'I know how to operate a forklift' ayaa ka xirfad badan 'I can operate a forklift.'
